title: En vs. Ett Noun Genders
subtitle: Mastering Sweden's two grammatical genders
keyPoint: Every Swedish noun belongs to either the common gender (en-words, roughly 75%) or the neuter gender (ett-words, roughly 25%).

useCases.label: Neuter Gender (Ett-words)
useCases.example: Vi bor i ett stort hus.

useCases.label: Indefinite Quantification
useCases.example: Hon har ett barn och en katt.

examples.en: Han dricker en kopp kaffe.
Det ligger ett brev på bordet.
Jag vill ha en smörgås, tack.
Vi hyr ett rum i Stockholm.
Hon läser en spännande bok.

mistakes.note: Most living things are common gender (en), so 'katt' takes the article 'en'.
'Äpple' is an inherent neuter noun, so it requires 'ett'.
'Bord' is a neuter noun and must be paired with 'ett'.

quiz.question: I see ___ car on the street.
quiz.explanation: 'Bil' is an en-word (common gender), so it takes the indefinite article 'en'.

quiz.question: Do you live in ___ house?
quiz.explanation: 'Hus' is an ett-word (neuter gender), requiring 'ett'.

quiz.question: Lisa reads ___ interesting book.
quiz.explanation: 'Bok' is an en-word, so we use 'en'.

quiz.question: He eats ___ red apple.
quiz.explanation: 'Äpple' is neuter, so the indefinite article is 'ett'.

tip: When learning new Swedish vocabulary, always memorize the noun together with its article ('en bil', 'ett hus') as one indivisible unit.

title: Suffix Definiteness
subtitle: How Swedish attaches 'the' directly to the noun
keyPoint: Swedish forms the definite form ('the') by attaching an ending (-en, -n, -et, -t) directly to the end of the noun.

examples.en: Bilen står parkerad utanför.
Huset är mycket gammalt.
Solen skiner idag.
Jag stänger fönstret nu.
Kaffet smakar fantastiskt.

mistakes.note: Swedish does not use a standalone article like 'the' for basic nouns; use the suffix '-en' instead.
'Katt' is an en-word, so its definite ending is '-en', never '-et'.
When an en-word already ends in a vowel, only add '-n', not '-en'.

quiz.question: ___ (The dog) is sleeping on the floor.
quiz.explanation: 'En hund' takes the suffix '-en' to become 'hunden'.

quiz.question: Where is ___ (the house)?
quiz.explanation: 'Ett hus' ends in a consonant and takes '-et', giving 'huset'.

quiz.question: ___ (The girl) sings well.
quiz.explanation: 'En flicka' ends in a vowel, so you attach just '-n' to get 'flickan'.

quiz.question: He washes ___ (the table).
quiz.explanation: 'Ett bord' takes the definite neuter suffix '-et', making 'bordet'.

tip: Think of the indefinite articles 'en' and 'ett' as flying around to the back of the word: 'en bil' becomes 'bil-en', and 'ett bord' becomes 'bord-et'!

title: V2 Rule in Main Clauses
subtitle: Keeping the finite verb in position two
keyPoint: In Swedish main declarative clauses, the finite verb MUST strictly be the second constituent, even when something other than the subject begins the sentence.

examples.en: På måndag börjar jag mitt nya jobb.
Nu förstår vi regeln ganska bra.
Han läser tidningen varje dag.
Klockan åtta vaknar barnen.
I morgon åker de till Malmö.

mistakes.note: If an adverb of time starts the clause, the verb must stay in position 2, forcing the subject into position 3.

mistakes.wrong: På kvällen vi tittar på tv.
mistakes.right: På kvällen tittar vi på tv.
mistakes.note: Swedish requires verb-subject inversion when the sentence begins with an adverbial phrase.
Place phrases trigger the V2 rule: the verb 'leker' must precede the subject 'barnen'.

quiz.question: Tomorrow ___ we to the cinema.
quiz.explanation: Starting with 'I morgon' (tomorrow) pushes the verb 'går' to the second spot, followed by 'vi'.

quiz.question: Now ___ the train.
quiz.explanation: With 'Nu' in position 1, the finite verb 'kommer' must take position 2 before 'tåget'.

quiz.question: In Sweden ___ coffee frequently.
quiz.explanation: After 'I Sverige', the verb 'dricker' must immediately follow in position 2.

quiz.question: Today ___ Maria to the market.
quiz.explanation: V2 inversion puts 'åker' in position 2 immediately after the adverb 'Idag'.

tip: Position 1 can be a single word like 'Idag' or a long phrase like 'Efter en mycket lång resa'—the verb must still be the very next element!

title: Present Tense Verb Groups
subtitle: Conjugating present verbs without person endings
keyPoint: Swedish verbs do not change for person or number (I, you, we all use the same form) and end in either -ar, -er, or -r in the present tense.

examples.en: Han studerar biologi vid universitetet.
Vi dricker te tillsammans.
De tror på framtiden.
Hon köper bröd varje lördag.
Jag lyssnar på musik.

mistakes.note: Present tense verbs in Swedish must end in '-r' (e.g. 'äter'), never bare stems without endings.
Even for plural subjects ('de'), the verb must take the present tense suffix '-r' ('talar').
Do not insert 'är' (is) as an auxiliary for present continuous actions; 'bor' covers both 'lives' and 'is living'.

quiz.question: She ___ Swedish at university. (tala)
quiz.explanation: Group 1 verbs replace infinitive '-a' with present ending '-ar' (talar).

quiz.question: We ___ a book right now. (läsa)
quiz.explanation: Group 2 verbs form the present tense with '-er' (läser).

quiz.question: Where do you ___? (bo)
quiz.explanation: Group 3 vowel-stem verbs add '-r' in the present tense (bor).

quiz.question: They ___ coffee every afternoon. (dricka)
quiz.explanation: 'Dricka' is a strong verb whose present form ends in '-er' (dricker).

tip: Swedish has no separate continuous tense (no 'is doing'). The simple present form 'jag springer' means both 'I run' and 'I am running'!

title: Adjective Agreement in the Indefinite
subtitle: Matching adjectives to en, ett, and plural nouns
keyPoint: Adjectives in the indefinite change form to match the head noun: base form for en-words, add -t for ett-words, and add -a for all plurals.

examples.en: Han kör en snabb bil.
Det är ett snabbt tåg.
De har mycket snabba cyklar.
Hon bär en varm jacka.
Rummet har ett stort fönster.

mistakes.wrong: Jag bor i ett stor hus.
mistakes.right: Jag bor i ett stort hus.
mistakes.note: Because 'hus' is an ett-word, the adjective 'stor' must take the neuter suffix '-t'.
Plural nouns require the adjective to end in '-a', regardless of original gender.
'Blomma' is an en-word, so keep the base adjective 'fin' without the neuter '-t'.

quiz.question: Peter lives in a ___ house. (stor)
quiz.explanation: 'Hus' is an ett-word, so 'stor' adds '-t' to become 'stort'.

quiz.question: She has a ___ jacket. (varm)
quiz.explanation: 'Jacka' is an en-word, so the adjective stays in its base form 'varm'.

quiz.question: They bought three ___ chairs. (ny)
quiz.explanation: Plural nouns (stolar) require the '-a' adjective ending (nya).

quiz.question: We drink ___ water. (kall - neuter)
quiz.explanation: 'Vatten' is neuter (ett vatten), so the adjective takes '-t' to become 'kallt'.

tip: Adjectives ending in double consonants simplify before '-t', so 'vass' (sharp) becomes 'vasst', while regular adjectives simply add '-t' ('grön' -> 'grönt').

title: The Five Plural Declensions
subtitle: Mastering indefinite plural noun endings in Swedish
keyPoint: Swedish nouns form their indefinite plurals using five main patterns: -or, -ar, -er, -n, and zero endings.

examples.en: Jag köper tre flaskor vatten.
Det står många stolar i rummet.
Hon läser flera böcker varje månad.
Vi plockar röda äpplen från trädet.
De äger fem gamla hus vid havet.

mistakes.note: Bok belongs to Group 3 and takes the plural ending -er with an umlaut shift, not the singular definite suffix -en.
Ett-words ending in a consonant (Group 5) do not add a suffix in the indefinite plural.
Ett-words ending in a vowel (Group 4) take -n, not -er.

quiz.question: Jag ser tre ___ på sjön.
quiz.explanation: 'En båt' is an en-word belonging to Group 2, which takes the plural ending -ar.

quiz.question: Vi behöver köpa fyra nya ___.
quiz.explanation: 'En stol' takes the Group 2 plural suffix -ar (stolar).

quiz.question: Han dricker två koppar kaffe och äter två ___.
quiz.explanation: 'Ett äpple' ends in a vowel and belongs to Group 4, forming the plural with -n.

quiz.question: I skogen finns det många höga ___.
quiz.explanation: 'Ett träd' is a neuter noun ending in a consonant, so its indefinite plural takes zero ending (träd).

tip: If an en-word ends in '-a', drop the '-a' and add '-or' almost 100% of the time (e.g., flicka -> flickor).

title: Double Definiteness (Den/Det/De + Noun Suffix)
subtitle: Combining front articles and noun suffixes with adjectives
keyPoint: When an adjective describes a definite noun, Swedish requires both a preceding definite article (den/det/de) and the definite noun ending.

examples.en: Den röda bilen kör snabbt.
Jag vill bo i det vita huset.
De gamla böckerna ligger på bordet.
Hon läser den intressanta boken.
Vi köpte det stora bordet igår.

mistakes.note: Double definiteness requires both the definite adjective ending (-a) and the noun suffix (-en).
Ett-words require the front article 'det', definite adjective form ending in -a, and suffix -et.
Plural nouns preceded by 'de' must also take their definite plural suffix (-na).

quiz.question: Jag gillar inte ___.
quiz.explanation: Mjölk is an en-word, requiring 'den', the definite adjective 'kalla', and suffix '-en'.

quiz.question: Vem äger ___?
quiz.explanation: Hus is an ett-word, requiring front article 'det' and the suffix '-et' on the noun.

quiz.question: Titta på ___ som simmar där borta.
quiz.explanation: Plural nouns need the article 'de', the adjective ending -a ('små' is already plural), and the suffix '-na'.

quiz.question: Vi känner redan ___.
quiz.explanation: Lärare is an en-word, so it takes 'den', definite adjective 'nya', and the noun ending '-n'.

tip: Think of it as sandwiching the adjective: Article (den/det/de) + Adjective (-a) + Suffix (-en/-et/-na).

title: Adverbial Placement in Subordinate Clauses (BIFF Rule)
subtitle: Where to place 'inte' and other adverbs in subordinate clauses
keyPoint: According to the BIFF rule (BIsats Inte Före Finita verbet), sentence adverbs like 'inte' must stand before the finite verb in subordinate clauses.

useCases.label: Causal Clause (eftersom)
useCases.example: Hon stannar hemma eftersom hon inte mår bra.

useCases.label: Conditional Clause (om)
useCases.example: Vi går ut om det inte regnar.

useCases.label: Reported Speech (att)
useCases.example: Han säger att han inte vet svaret.

examples.en: Han stannar hemma eftersom han inte mår bra.
Jag vet att du inte tycker om fisk.
Vi går en promenad om det inte snöar.
Hon frågade varför vi inte kom igår.
Det är synd att de inte kan komma.

mistakes.wrong: Jag är ledsen eftersom jag kommer inte.
mistakes.right: Jag är ledsen eftersom jag inte kommer.
mistakes.note: In subordinate clauses introduced by conjunctions like 'eftersom', 'inte' must precede the finite verb.

mistakes.wrong: Han sa att han förstod inte frågan.
mistakes.right: Han sa att han inte förstod frågan.
mistakes.note: Follow the BIFF rule: 'inte' comes before 'förstod' inside 'att' clauses.

mistakes.wrong: Om du vill inte, behöver du inte.
mistakes.right: Om du inte vill, behöver du inte.
mistakes.note: In the conditional subclause 'om du...', place 'inte' before the modal verb 'vill'.

quiz.question: Jag ringer dig om jag ___ tid imorgon.
quiz.explanation: The BIFF rule states that 'inte' must go before the finite verb ('har') in a subordinate clause introduced by 'om'.

quiz.question: Hon berättade att hon ___ filmen.
quiz.explanation: 'Att' introduces a subordinate clause, placing 'inte' directly before the finite verb 'såg'.

quiz.question: Vi stannar inne därför att det ___ varmt ute.
quiz.explanation: In subordinate clauses with 'därför att', the adverb 'inte' precedes the finite verb 'är'.

quiz.question: Vet du varför Peter ___ till festen igår?
quiz.explanation: In an indirect question clause introduced by 'varför', 'inte' precedes the finite verb 'kom'.

tip: Remember the acronym BIFF: I BIsats kommer 'Inte' Före Finita verbet.

title: Preteritum vs. Supinum (Perfekt)
subtitle: Choosing between simple past and present perfect in Swedish
keyPoint: Preteritum narrates completed events tied to a specific past time, while supinum combines with 'har' (perfekt) to express experiences or ongoing relevance.

examples.en: Igår köpte jag en ny dator.
Jag har redan köpt biljetterna.
Förra veckan såg vi en fantastisk film.
Har du någonsin varit i Sverige?
Han skrev ett långt brev i morse.

mistakes.note: Specific past time markers like 'igår' require preteritum, not perfekt.
You cannot use 'har + supinum' with finished, definite past time adverbials.
After auxiliary 'har', Swedish requires the supinum ending in -t ('bott'), not the past tense 'bodde'.

quiz.question: Förra året ___ vi till Spanien på semester.
quiz.explanation: 'Förra året' indicates a completed, specific time in the past, demanding the preteritum 'reste'.

quiz.question: Jag kan inte hitta min plånbok; jag tror att jag ___ den.
quiz.explanation: The loss is relevant right now in the present, which requires perfekt formed with 'har' + supinum 'tappat'.

quiz.question: Hon har redan ___ frukost idag.
quiz.explanation: The auxiliary 'har' must be paired with the supinum form 'ätit', not the preteritum 'åt'.

quiz.question: Vad ___ du klockan åtta i morse?
quiz.explanation: 'I morse' sets a finished past time point, requiring preteritum 'gjorde'.

tip: Supinum is unique to Swedish: unlike past participles, it only ends in -t (never inflects for gender/number) and only follows 'ha'.

title: Modal Auxiliaries and Bare Infinitives
subtitle: Expressing ability, necessity, and desire without 'att'
keyPoint: Core Swedish modal verbs take a bare infinitive directly without the infinitive marker 'att'.

useCases.label: Ability (kan)
useCases.example: Hon kan tala tre språk flytande.

useCases.label: Obligation (måste)
useCases.example: Vi måste gå hem tidigt ikväll.

examples.en: Jag vill äta lunch klockan tolv.
Han kan simma mycket snabbt.
Vi måste städa lägenheten idag.
Du får låna min cykel imorgon.
Ska vi gå på bio ikväll?

mistakes.note: Never place the infinitive marker 'att' after modal verbs like 'vill'.
'Kan' takes a bare infinitive; omit 'att' completely.
'Måste' links directly with the bare infinitive 'arbeta'.

quiz.question: Jag kan tyvärr inte ___ på fredag.
quiz.explanation: The modal auxiliary 'kan' must be followed directly by a bare infinitive without 'att'.

quiz.question: Vad ska du ___ till middag ikväll?
quiz.explanation: The modal verb 'ska' requires the bare infinitive 'laga'.

quiz.question: Alla studenter måste ___ provet innan klockan tre.
quiz.explanation: 'Måste' takes the bare infinitive without the infinitive marker 'att'.

quiz.question: Här får man inte ___ bilen över natten.
quiz.explanation: The permission modal 'får' requires the bare infinitive 'parkera'.

tip: English says 'want TO sleep', but Swedish strictly drops 'to': 'vill sova' (never 'vill att sova').

title: Particle Verbs vs. Prepositional Verbs
subtitle: Stress the particle to transform the verb's meaning completely.
keyPoint: In Swedish particle verbs, the stress falls squarely on the particle rather than the verb stem, shifting the meaning entirely.

examples.en: Han tycker om att resa på sommaren.
Skriv under kontraktet här.
Vi måste ställa in mötet i dag.
Hon ser på teve varje kväll.
Tåget kom fram i tid.

mistakes.note: Pronounce 'om' with primary stress, not 'tycker', or native listeners will hear a preposition instead of the verb 'to like'.
Unlike English, verbal particles in Swedish typically stay directly adjacent to the finite verb before any definite noun object.

mistakes.right: Vi lyssnar på musik på kvällen.
mistakes.note: 'Lyssna' requires the preposition 'på' when specifying the object of listening.

quiz.question: Choose the particle verb phrase meaning 'to cancel the concert':
quiz.explanation: 'Ställa in' is the idiomatic particle verb meaning 'to cancel'.

quiz.question: In 'De tycker om glass', where does the main stress fall?
quiz.explanation: In Swedish particle verbs, the stress systematically falls on the particle ('om').

quiz.question: Which sentence means 'She turned off the radio'?
quiz.explanation: 'Stänga av' means to turn off/switch off, and the particle directly follows the verb before the noun object.

quiz.question: Complete the sentence to mean 'He signed the letter': Han ___ brevet.
quiz.explanation: 'Skriva under' is the lexicalized particle verb meaning 'to sign'.

tip: Listen for the beat: if the short word after the verb carries the strongest stress, it is a particle that changes the dictionary definition.

title: Sin/Sitt/Sina vs. Hans/Hennes/Deras
subtitle: Use sin/sitt/sina only when the owner is the third-person subject of that exact clause.
keyPoint: Use reflexive possessives (sin/sitt/sina) when the owner is the subject of the same clause, but use hans/hennes/deras when referring to someone else or inside the subject itself.

examples.en: Anna älskar sin hund väldigt mycket.
Oskar sålde sitt gamla piano.
Föräldrarna hjälper sina barn med läxan.
Lars ringde till hans fru i går.
Hennes bror studerar i Lund.

mistakes.note: 'Sin/sitt/sina' can NEVER be part of the grammatical subject of the clause; use hans/hennes/deras instead.
If Per loves his own wife, you must use 'sin'. Using 'hans' implies Per loves another man's wife.
'Vänner' is plural, so the reflexive pronoun must agree in number and take 'sina'.

quiz.question: Peter drove ___ car home (his own car, ett-word: fordon/bil). 'Peter körde ___ bil hem.'
quiz.explanation: 'Bil' is an en-word (common gender) and belongs to the subject Peter, so use 'sin'.

quiz.question: Fill the blank: '___ syster bor i Göteborg.' (Talking about Johan's sister)
quiz.explanation: The possessor is part of the subject noun phrase itself; 'sin' cannot appear in the subject position.

quiz.question: Sara and Lisa pack ___ bags (plural, their own). 'Sara och Lisa packar ___ väskor.'
quiz.explanation: 'Väskor' is plural and refers back to the plural subject 'Sara och Lisa', requiring 'sina'.

quiz.question: Which sentence means 'Kalle borrowed someone else's coat'?
quiz.explanation: 'Hans' indicates that the jacket belongs to someone other than the subject Kalle.

tip: Always identify the grammatical subject first: if the possessor IS that subject, choose sin/sitt/sina; if not (or if it is inside the subject itself), use hans/hennes/deras.

title: Reflexive Verbs and the Pronoun 'Sig'
subtitle: Inflect reflexive objects to match 1st/2nd persons, and use 'sig' for all 3rd persons.
keyPoint: Swedish reflexive verbs require standard object pronouns for 1st and 2nd persons (mig, dig, oss, er) and the invariant reflexive pronoun 'sig' for all third-person subjects.

useCases.label: Emotional & Mental States
useCases.example: Hon känner sig trött efter jobbet.

examples.en: Jag måste skynda mig till bussen.
Han sätter sig på stolen i hörnet.
Vi känner oss glada över resultatet.
Barnen lägger sig klockan åtta.
Hur mår du? Rakar du dig varje dag?

mistakes.note: 'Sig' is strictly for third person (han, hon, den, det, de). First person 'jag' requires 'mig'.
'Dem' is a non-reflexive object pronoun; when referring back to the 3rd person subject 'de', use 'sig'.
The first-person plural 'vi' requires the matching reflexive pronoun 'oss'.

quiz.question: Complete the sentence: 'Hon känner ___ inte så pigg i dag.'
quiz.explanation: The 3rd-person singular subject 'hon' requires the reflexive pronoun 'sig'.

quiz.question: Complete the sentence: 'Nu måste vi skynda ___!'
quiz.explanation: The subject 'vi' matches with the 1st-person plural reflexive pronoun 'oss'.

quiz.question: Complete the sentence: 'Varför lägger ni ___ så sent?'
quiz.explanation: Second person plural 'ni' takes 'er' as its reflexive object pronoun.

quiz.question: Which sentence is grammatically correct?
options: Han lär dem sig tala svenska.
quiz.explanation: 'Lära sig' means to learn (literally 'to teach oneself'); matching 'han' requires 'sig'.

tip: Think of 'sig' as Swedish for 'himself/herself/itself/themselves'—use it only when the subject is 3rd person.

title: Morphological S-Passive vs. Periphrastic Bli-Passive
subtitle: Use s-passives for notices, rules, and states; use bli-passives for dynamic, single events.
keyPoint: The morphological s-passive is favored for rules, instructions, recipes, and timeless facts, while the 'bli + past participle' passive highlights dynamic, momentary events.

cells: Concrete single events, change of state
Han blev påkörd av en bil.
Resulting static state after an action

examples.en: Maten serveras klockan tolv.
Bron förstördes av stormen.
Han blev vald till ordförande i går.
Detta problem måste lösas omedelbart.
Fönstret krossades under festen.

mistakes.note: Never combine 'bli' with an -s passive verb; use either 'serveras' or 'blir serverad'.
After 'bli', the following verb must be an inflected past participle ('sparkad'), not an s-passive infinitive.
Passive infinitives after modal verbs like 'måste' require the -s ending: 'öppnas'.

quiz.question: Which sentence is the most natural for a sign: 'The door closes at 21:00'?
quiz.explanation: Timeless routines, signs, and official hours strongly favor the morphological s-passive ('stängs').

quiz.question: Complete the dynamic event: 'Mannen ___ av polisen efter rånet.'
quiz.explanation: A dynamic singular event completed by an agent ('av polisen') commonly uses 'blev + past participle'.

quiz.question: How do you form the passive infinitive after 'kan' with 'köpa'?
quiz.explanation: The passive infinitive adds -s to the active infinitive stem ('köpa' -> 'köpas').

quiz.question: What is the difference between 'Fönstret stängdes' and 'Fönstret är stängt'?
options: They are completely identical in every context.
The first describes the action occurring; the second describes the resulting state.
The second means someone will close it tomorrow.
The first can only be used with human subjects.
quiz.explanation: S-passive conveys the passive process/action; 'vara + past participle' expresses the resulting static condition.

tip: Look at the context: signs, menus, recipes, and recurring routines almost always use the short -s passive, while dramatic incidents use 'bli + participle'.

title: Inflection of the Past Participle
subtitle: Decline participles like adjectives (en, ett, plural) when paired with vara or bli.
keyPoint: While the supinum used with 'ha' is invariant (-t), the past participle functions as an adjective and must agree in gender and number with the noun it modifies.

examples.en: Dörren är stängd för dagen.
Ett brev blev skrivet av professorn.
Alla fönster är tvättade nu.
Maten är redan lagad.
Bordet blev dukat av barnen.

mistakes.note: 'Skrivit' is the invariable supinum used after 'har'. With 'är' (en-word), the participle inflects as 'skriven'.
Take care to avoid using singular '-d/-t' when the subject is plural ('husen' -> 'sålda').
After auxiliary 'ha', you must always use the invariant supinum ('stängt'), never an inflected participle.

quiz.question: Which form completes: 'Äpplet är ___.' (äta - strong verb; ett äpple)?
quiz.explanation: The strong verb past participle declines as -en (en-word), -et (ett-word), -na (plural). For 'äpplet' (ett-word), choose 'ätet'.

quiz.question: Complete the plural sentence: 'Rapporterna är redan ___.' (skriva)
quiz.explanation: 'Rapporterna' is plural, requiring the plural participle ending '-na'.

quiz.question: What is the difference between 'har stängt' and 'är stängd'?
options: 'har stängt' is the invariant supinum tense; 'är stängd' is an inflected participle describing state.
'är stängd' can only be used with animate subjects.
quiz.explanation: After 'ha' use the supinum (-t); after 'vara/bli' the participle agrees like an adjective with the subject.

quiz.question: Complete with 'måla' (Group 1): 'Stolarna blev ___ vita.'
quiz.explanation: 'Stolarna' is plural; Group 1 verbs inflect as -ad (en), -at (ett), -ade (plural).

tip: Test the auxiliary: if you see 'har' or 'hade', use the unchanging supinum (-t); if you see 'är', 'var', or 'blev', treat the participle like an adjective and match the noun.

title: The -ande/-ende Present Participle
subtitle: Forming descriptive participles and avoiding English continuous tense transfer
keyPoint: Swedish present participles ending in -ande or -ende function purely as adjectives or adverbs, never as progressive verb tenses like English '-ing'.

useCases.label: Attributive Adjective
useCases.example: Vi såg ett lysande exempel på gott ledarskap.

useCases.label: Manner Adverb with Motion Verbs
useCases.example: Barnen kom skrattande ut från klassrummet.

examples.en: Ett leende barn mötte oss i dörren.
Mannen blev sittande kvar på bänken.
Hon svarade med en nickande rörelse.
Det var ett avgörande ögonblick för matchen.
Fågeln flög sjungande genom skogen.

mistakes.wrong: Jag är läsande en bok nu.
mistakes.note: Never translate English continuous 'am reading' with a participle; use simple present 'läser' or 'håller på att läsa'.
Verbs with roots ending in a stressed vowel take -ende rather than -ande.
Swedish uses the infinitive with 'att' where English uses gerundial '-ing' as an activity noun.

quiz.question: How do you correctly say 'I am eating right now' in natural Swedish?
options: Jag håller på ätande just nu.
Jag är att äta just nu.
quiz.explanation: Swedish expresses ongoing actions using the standard present tense (äter) or 'håller på att äta', never 'är ätande'.

quiz.question: Choose the correct participle form for 'tro' (to believe):
quiz.explanation: Verbs ending in a stressed root vowel take the suffix -ende (tro -> troende).

quiz.question: Complete: 'Pojken kom ___ mot sin mamma.' (running)
quiz.explanation: Motion verbs like 'komma' take a present participle in -ande/-ende to describe simultaneous manner.

quiz.question: Identify the incorrect Swedish sentence:
options: Hon gav mig ett värmande leende.
Min bror är arbetande i Stockholm just nu.
quiz.explanation: 'Är arbetande' is an incorrect literal translation of 'is working'; it must be 'Min bror arbetar i Stockholm just nu'.

tip: If you are tempted to use -ande/-ende as a finite verb after 'är' or 'var', stop! Use simple present/past instead, or 'håller på att + infinitive' for continuous focus.

title: Topicalization and Cleft Sentences (Det är ... som)
subtitle: Fronting elements with V2 word order and clefting for contrastive emphasis
keyPoint: Fronting any non-subject element triggers obligatory V2 inversion, while cleft sentences use 'Det är/var X som...' to isolate and emphasize a specific focus.

cells: Emphasis on time; strict V2 inversion
Det var Lisa som köpte bilen.
Det var igår som Lisa köpte bilen.

useCases.label: Time/Place Fronting
useCases.example: I morgon åker hela familjen till fjällen.

useCases.label: Contrastive Focus Cleft
useCases.example: Det är min syster som bor i Göteborg, inte jag.

useCases.label: Correcting False Assumptions
useCases.example: Det var faktiskt Peter som ringde polisen.

examples.en: Den här boken har jag läst två gånger.
examples.highlight: Den här boken har jag läst

examples.en: Det är Johan som talar flytande spanska.
På fredag ska vi äta middag tillsammans.
Det var i Stockholm som vi träffades första gången.
examples.highlight: Det var i Stockholm som vi träffades

examples.en: Henne känner jag inte alls.

mistakes.note: Swedish strictly enforces V2 word order; fronting an adverbial forces the finite verb before the subject.

mistakes.wrong: Det är honom vem vann tävlingen.
mistakes.right: Det är han som vann tävlingen.
mistakes.note: Swedish clefts use 'som' as the universal subordinator; interrogative 'vem' cannot be used here.

mistakes.wrong: Det är i morgon när vi ska resa.
mistakes.right: Det är i morgon som vi ska resa.
mistakes.note: Even when emphasizing time in a cleft sentence, the relative connector remains 'som', not 'när'.

quiz.question: Front the object: 'Jag gillar inte den här filmen.' -> '___'
options: Den här filmen gillar jag inte.
Den här filmen jag gillar inte.
Den här filmen inte gillar jag.
Den här filmen jag inte gillar.
quiz.explanation: Fronting the object 'Den här filmen' places the finite verb 'gillar' in second position, followed by the subject 'jag'.

quiz.question: Complete the cleft sentence to emphasize 'Maria': 'Det är Maria ___ ringde.'
quiz.explanation: Cleft sentences (brytningar) in Swedish invariably employ 'som' to introduce the subordinate clause.

quiz.question: Choose the correctly inverted sentence after fronting an adverbial:
options: Plötsligt hörde vi ett märkligt ljud.
Plötsligt vi hörde ett märkligt ljud.
Plötsligt vi ett märkligt ljud hörde.
Plötsligt hörde ett märkligt ljud vi.
quiz.explanation: Adverbial first triggers V2: Adverbial (Plötsligt) + Finite Verb (hörde) + Subject (vi).

quiz.question: Which sentence correctly clefts 'i fjol' (last year)?
options: Det var i fjol när vi flyttade hit.
Det var i fjol som vi flyttade hit.
Det var i fjol då vi flyttade hit.
Det är i fjol att vi flyttade hit.
quiz.explanation: 'Det var [tid] som...' is the correct construction; Swedish cleft clauses rely on 'som', not 'när' or 'då'.

tip: Whenever you begin a Swedish sentence with anything other than the subject, check immediately if your finite verb sits safely in slot 2!

title: Relative Pronoun 'Som' and Preposition Stranding
subtitle: Mastering invariable 'som', genitive 'vars', and sentence-final prepositions
keyPoint: Swedish uses the invariable relative marker 'som' for both people and things, stranding any governing prepositions at the very end of the relative clause.

cells: Huset som vi bor i är gammalt.
The city where he grew up...

useCases.label: Subject / Object Relative
useCases.example: Boken som ligger på bordet är min.

useCases.label: Preposition Stranding
useCases.example: Flickan som han pratade med heter Sara.

useCases.label: Genitive Antecedent
useCases.example: Vi träffade en man vars son studerar i Uppsala.

examples.en: Datorn som jag köpte igår fungerar perfekt.
Här är restaurangen som vi åt på i lördags.
Det var ett problem vars lösning krävde tid.
Mannen som du ser där borta är min farbror.
Filmen som alla pratar om har vunnit flera priser.

mistakes.wrong: Mannen med vem jag talade är snäll.
mistakes.right: Mannen som jag talade med är snäll.
mistakes.note: Swedish avoids pied-piping like 'med vem'; use 'som' and strand the preposition 'med' at the end.

mistakes.wrong: Huset vilkets tak läcker är sålt.
mistakes.right: Huset vars tak läcker är sålt.
mistakes.note: Use 'vars' for relative possession ('whose') for both persons and inanimate nouns.

mistakes.wrong: Kvinnan som bor i Malmö hon är läkare.
mistakes.right: Kvinnan som bor i Malmö är läkare.
mistakes.note: Do not insert a redundant resumptive pronoun ('hon') after the relative clause.

quiz.question: Fill in the blank: 'Tåget ___ vi väntar på är försenat.'
quiz.explanation: 'Som' is the universal restrictive relative pronoun for both objects and persons.

quiz.question: Choose the natural Swedish phrasing for 'The boy whose dog ran away':
quiz.explanation: 'Vars' is the relative possessive pronoun meaning 'whose'. 'Vems' is only interrogative.

quiz.question: Which sentence demonstrates correct Swedish preposition stranding?
options: Det här är pennan med vilken jag skrev.
Det här är pennan jag skrev med den.
Det här är pennan som jag skrev med.
Det här är pennan som med jag skrev.
quiz.explanation: In Swedish relative clauses, the governing preposition ('med') is stranded at the end of the clause after 'som'.

quiz.question: Fill in: 'Skolan ___ mina barn går har en stor trädgård.'
quiz.explanation: 'Där' refers to a static location ('where'); 'dit' denotes movement toward ('whither').

tip: Never translate 'the person with whom' literally. Swedish overwhelmingly prefers 'personen som jag pratade med', stranding the preposition naturally at the end.

title: Deponent and Reciprocal S-Verbs
subtitle: Active meaning in passive packaging: deponents vs. reciprocal actions
keyPoint: Deponent verbs end in -s across all tenses but have exclusively active meanings, whereas reciprocal s-verbs express mutual 'each other' actions.

useCases.label: Deponent Mental State
useCases.example: Jag minns fortfarande vår första resa till Gotland.

useCases.label: Reciprocal Social Action
useCases.example: Vi träffas på caféet klockan tre.

useCases.label: Deponent Habitual Activity
useCases.example: Hon svettas mycket när hon springer.

examples.en: Vi hoppas att det slutar regna snart.
Han låtsades som om ingenting hade hänt.
Hur trivs du på din nya arbetsplats?
De kramades länge på flygplatsen.
Jag minns inte vad han heter i efternamn.

mistakes.wrong: Jag hoppar att du mår bra.
mistakes.right: Jag hoppas att du mår bra.
mistakes.note: 'Hoppa' means to jump physically; 'hoppas' is the deponent verb meaning to hope.
'Minnas' is deponent, not a passive voice; it cannot take an agent with 'av'.
Reciprocal -s verbs already encapsulate 'each other' / reflexive meaning; adding 'oss' is ungrammatical.

quiz.question: Complete the sentence: 'Jag ___ verkligen på mitt nya jobb.' (thrive/enjoy)
quiz.explanation: The present tense of the deponent verb 'trivas' is 'trivs'.

quiz.question: What is the past tense of 'hoppas' (to hope)?
quiz.explanation: 'Hoppas' belongs to group 1; its preterite form retains the deponent ending: 'hoppades'.

quiz.question: Which verb is reciprocal rather than strictly deponent?
quiz.explanation: 'Enas' implies mutual consensus between two or more parties ('to come to an agreement with each other').

quiz.question: Identify the incorrect usage of a deponent verb:
quiz.explanation: The verb 'låtsas' is deponent in standard Swedish and must keep its -s in the present tense: 'Han låtsas'.

tip: Remember: 'hoppa' = to jump, 'hoppas' = to hope. Forgetting the -s turns a heartfelt wish into physical bouncing!

title: Modal and Pragmatic Particles (Ju, Väl, Nog, Kanske)
subtitle: Fine-tuning conversational nuance, epistemic stance, and shared knowledge
keyPoint: Swedish modal particles like 'ju', 'väl', and 'nog' signal shared assumptions, tentativeness, or probability, placed in the main clause adverbial slot.

cells: Du vet ju vad som hände.
It will probably / surely work out.

useCases.label: Invoking Common Knowledge (ju)
useCases.example: Det är ju söndag idag, så butiken är stängd.

useCases.label: Hedging / Checking Assumption (väl)
useCases.example: Du har väl inte glömt nycklarna?

useCases.label: Cautious Optimism / Probability (nog)
useCases.example: Tåget är nog bara några minuter sent.

examples.en: Vi kan inte gå nu, det regnar ju!
Han har väl redan läst rapporten?
Jag tror att hon kommer nog att klara provet.
Du känner ju min bror sedan tidigare.
Det blir nog fint väder till helgen.

mistakes.note: Particles like 'ju' cannot stand first as sentence adverbs; they occupy the middle adverbial position after the verb.

mistakes.wrong: Du kommer väl, kommer du inte?
mistakes.note: 'Väl' already acts as an epistemic tag question ('right? / aren't you?'); adding an English-style tag is redundant.

mistakes.wrong: Han är nog inte sjuk, han är död!
mistakes.note: 'Nog' implies 'probably/supposedly'; do not use it when you state certain, absolute facts.

quiz.question: Which particle best conveys 'as everyone knows / obviously': 'Det är ___ inte tillåtet att röka här.'
quiz.explanation: 'Ju' appeals to shared, self-evident knowledge ('as you know / obviously').

quiz.question: You expect an affirmative answer to 'You haven't told anyone, right?'. Choose the best particle: 'Du har ___ inte sagt något till någon?'
quiz.explanation: 'Väl' turns a statement into a gentle verification tag expecting confirmation from the listener.

quiz.question: Where should 'ju' be placed in this subordinate clause: '...eftersom hon [1] har [2] varit [3] sjuk [4]?'
quiz.explanation: In Swedish subordinate clauses, modal adverbs obey the BIFF rule (Bifogade satser: Inte/adverb Före Finita verbet) and precede the finite verb: '...eftersom hon ju har varit sjuk'.

quiz.question: Choose the best particle for tentative reassurance: 'Oroa dig inte, det löser sig ___.'
quiz.explanation: 'Nog' conveys comforting probability or cautious optimism ('probably / surely').

tip: Keep the BIFF rule in mind: in main clauses, particles follow the finite verb ('Han kommer ju'); in subordinate clauses, they jump in FRONT of it ('...eftersom han ju kommer').
